title: The Baseline
hook: A gesture means nothing until you know what that body does when nothing is happening, and almost nobody bothers to find out.
why:
Picture the second interview for a job you want. Across the table the hiring manager keeps her arms folded, answers in short sentences and barely smiles. You spend forty minutes trying to win her back. You talk too much, you oversell, and you leave convinced you failed. A week later you learn that she folds her arms in every meeting, speaks that way to everyone, and rated you the strongest candidate she saw. Nothing in her body was about you. You read a stranger against a template, the generic person you imagine everyone to be, and the template lied.

This is the most common error in reading people, and it is not a shortage of attention. It is a missing reference. A signal is a change, and a change needs something to change from. Without a baseline, every habit looks like a message, every fidget looks like nerves, and every quiet person looks displeased. With one, most of what you see sorts itself into noise you can ignore, and the little that remains becomes a precise question you can ask. The baseline is not one technique among many in this book. Every other chapter assumes it.

teach.h: A signal exists only against a baseline.
teach.p:
Every reading you make is a comparison, whether you know it or not. When you think *he looks nervous*, you are comparing him with something: with how you imagine a calm person looks, with how you would look, or with how he looked an hour ago. Only the last comparison is worth much. The first two smuggle in a template, and templates are built from your own habits, your own culture and whatever you absorbed from films.

Paul Ekman, who spent decades studying the face and deception, named one version of this mistake the Brokaw hazard, after the television interviewer Tom Brokaw, who had said he watched for convoluted, evasive answers as a sign of lying. Ekman's point was that some people are convoluted and evasive all the time. Their manner tells you about their style, not about the question. The hazard is failing to allow for individual differences, and the cure is a baseline: a working picture of how this particular person behaves when nothing in particular is at stake.

Think of a friend who talks with his hands. If one evening his hands lie still in his lap while he tells you his week was fine, the stillness is information. In a man who never gestures, the same stillness is nothing. The posture is identical and the meaning is not, because meaning lives in the difference. That is why this book never offers a list of what gestures mean. A list can describe postures. It cannot tell you what is normal for the person in front of you, and without that it cannot tell you anything.

In practice a baseline answers four questions. How does this person sit or stand when settled? What do their hands do: illustrate, rest, fidget, touch the face? How fast and how loud do they speak, and where do they pause? Where do their eyes go when they think? You will not have all four answers at once, and you do not need them. You need enough to recognise a departure.
teach.disconfirm: If you find yourself confidently reading someone you have never seen at rest, you are using a template, not a baseline. The test is simple: could you describe how this person usually stands, gestures and speaks? If you could not, any deviation you think you see is a deviation from your own assumptions.
teach.pullQuote: The posture is identical and the meaning is not, because meaning lives in the difference.

teach.h: A baseline is a range, not a pose.
teach.p:
The word suggests a single line, but a person at rest is never still. They shift their weight, cross and uncross their legs, touch their face, glance at the window. A baseline is the range those movements occupy and the rate at which they happen. Get this wrong and you will treat ordinary fluctuation as a signal.

Consider how often people touch their own faces. In one observational study, Yen Lee Angela Kwok and her colleagues filmed medical students during lectures and counted: on average each student touched their face 23 times an hour. That is the background rate in a room of attentive adults with nothing in particular on their minds. If you watch someone for five minutes and see two face touches, you have seen nothing at all. If you watch the same person for twenty minutes, see almost none, and then see six in the ninety seconds after a particular remark, you may have seen something. The touch did not change. The rate did.

So record rates and ranges. *Touches his jaw two or three times a minute. Bounces his right knee while he listens and stops when he talks. Sits back with an arm over the chair and leans in when interested.* Notes like these describe a territory rather than a position, and they let you say with some confidence that a later behaviour falls outside it.

Ranges also tell you how much to trust your own eyes. A person whose resting range already includes a great deal of self-touch, foot movement and shifting has a noisy baseline, and small changes in them are hard to see and easy to invent. A very still person has a quiet baseline, where small changes stand out. Neither is better. Knowing which you are dealing with tells you how loudly a change has to speak before you listen.
teach.disconfirm: If a behaviour you flagged as a departure turns out to recur at about the same rate through the rest of the conversation, it was part of the range all along. Ten more minutes of watching is the cheapest test in this book.

teach.h: The same person has several baselines.
teach.p:
You do not have one way of sitting. You have one for your manager's office, one for your sofa, one for your father's kitchen table and one for a first date. Each is real and each is a baseline. When observers forget this, they take a baseline in one setting, apply it in another, and read the difference between the settings as a message about the moment.

Researchers on interviewing have made the same point formally. Aldert Vrij, who has studied deception for three decades, criticises a common interviewing practice: chat with someone about neutral topics to establish a baseline, then compare that with their behaviour during questions about the matter at hand. The two conversations differ in stakes, in difficulty, in emotion and in how closely the person is being watched, so behaviour differs in honest and dishonest people alike. The comparison tells you that hard questions are hard, which you knew. Vrij argues instead for a comparable baseline, taken under conditions as close as possible to the ones you care about.

For ordinary life the lesson is short. Compare like with like. If your colleague seems tense in the Monday budget meeting, compare her with herself in earlier budget meetings, not with herself at Friday drinks. If your brother is quiet at your parents' house, compare him with how he usually is at your parents' house, where he may have been quiet since he was twelve.

It also means a baseline expires. A man who has recently lost his job, his marriage or his sleep has a new resting state, and your old picture of him is out of date. When something large has changed in someone's life, start again.
teach.disconfirm: If the behaviour you noticed also appears when the same person is in the same kind of setting with nothing at stake, it belongs to the setting, not to the moment. Before you interpret a change, check that you are not comparing two different rooms.

teach.h: The first minutes measure the room, not the person.
teach.p:
Almost everyone is less settled at the start of an encounter than twenty minutes in. A new room, a new person, uncertainty about what is expected: all of it shows. Ankles hook under the chair, hands look for something to hold, the voice rides a little higher and the laugh comes a little quicker. Then, unless something keeps the stakes high, the body settles into its usual range.

If you take your baseline in those first minutes you will mistake the novelty for the person, and then misread the settling itself, seeing someone warm to you when they have merely warmed to the room. This costs people in job interviews, first dates and first meetings with clients, where both sides form firm impressions in exactly the window where behaviour is least representative.

A well-known line of research, begun by Nalini Ambady and Robert Rosenthal, found that strangers watching very short silent clips of teachers, thin slices of a few seconds, could predict those teachers' end-of-term ratings surprisingly well. It is tempting to take this as licence to read people quickly. Look closer. Those judgments concern broad, stable impressions such as warmth or confidence, pooled across several observers whose errors cancel out. They are not one observer's guess about what one person feels at one moment. Thin slices show that first impressions are consistent, not that they are right about anyone's state.

The practical rule: hold your reading of anyone loosely for the first ten or fifteen minutes. Watch for the moment they settle, the exhale, the lean back, the hands finding their usual place. That moment is where the baseline begins.
teach.disconfirm: If someone never settles, even after twenty minutes in a setting that should not threaten them, the novelty explanation fails. Either their baseline really is restless or something in the situation keeps the stakes high for them. Both are worth knowing, and neither is a conclusion yet.

teach.h: Record change, timing and duration, and nothing else yet.
teach.p:
Once you have a baseline you are looking for departures from it. Each departure has three properties worth writing down, and at first almost nothing else is.

Change: what moved, and in which direction. Not *he got defensive*, but *his arms went from loosely folded to gripped and his shoulders rose*. Describe the body, not your theory of the mind inside it. The discipline of plain description is what keeps your later interpretation honest.

Timing: what had just happened. A change that follows a specific question, name or topic within a second or two tells you far more than one that drifts in over a minute. Researchers who study emotional expression, Ekman among them, treat the timing of an expression relative to what prompted it as central evidence. If you cannot say what a change followed, you have not yet seen a signal, only a variation.

Duration: how long it lasted before the person returned to range. A brief departure that resolves in seconds suggests something registered and was absorbed. A shift that lasts the rest of the conversation suggests that the situation itself has changed for them. Both matter, differently.

Notice what is missing from the list: meaning. You are not yet allowed to say what the change means. That comes later, after you have checked it against other channels, against the context and against at least one alternative explanation. Write *at the mention of the move he stopped gesturing for about thirty seconds*, and you have something you can test. Write *he hates the idea of the move*, and you have a conclusion you will defend instead of examine.
teach.disconfirm: If you cannot name what a change followed, or it fades back into the person's range when you look again, treat it as variation. A departure that does not survive a second look was not one.
teach.pullQuote: Describe the body, not your theory of the mind inside it.

teach.p:
You are part of every scene you observe. If you arrive at a meeting short of sleep, anxious about the outcome or angry about something else, you will see a different room from the one a rested, neutral observer would see. This is not a moral failing; it is how perception works. The psychologist Joseph Forgas spent years documenting what he called affect infusion: mood seeps into our judgments of other people, and it seeps in most when the judgment is complex and the evidence ambiguous. Reading bodies is nearly always both.

So before you take anyone else's baseline, take your own. Where are your shoulders? Is your breath high in the chest or low? Is your jaw set? What do you want to be true about the person you are about to read? A man hoping his boss is pleased will find pleasure in her face, and a man who expects criticism will find that instead. The body you bring into the room is the lens you see it through.

Your own baseline matters for a second reason: you change what you observe. If you sit forward and stare, people become self-conscious, and their behaviour shifts toward a guardedness that you then dutifully record. Observation done well is quiet, side-on and intermittent. You watch the way you would watch weather from a window, not the way you would watch a suspect.

There is a reason the chapters on the inner world sit beside this one, and the chapters on discipline end with one called The Quiet Body. The best readers are not the ones with the sharpest eyes. They are the ones whose own state disturbs the reading least.
teach.disconfirm: If two observers with different moods and different stakes see the same change at the same moment, your own state is probably not producing it. If only you see it, and especially if it confirms what you feared, check yourself before you check them.

teach.h: A baseline is a hypothesis, and attention is not permission.
teach.p:
Everything you write down about how someone usually behaves is a guess built from a sample. The sample is small, it was taken in particular settings, and it was filtered through your attention, which catches some things and misses others. Treat your baseline as a working model: useful, provisional, and to be revised the moment it predicts badly. If you expected your friend to fidget through a long dinner and he sat still for two hours, your model of him is wrong, not his behaviour.

People also change. They recover, age, grieve, fall in love, start medication, stop drinking. The man whose baseline you learned five years ago may no longer exist. Long familiarity is no protection. Couples married for decades still misread each other, often because each is reading against a version of the other that is years out of date.

Finally, a baseline is a form of attention, and attention can tip into surveillance. The point of knowing how someone usually is, in this book, is to notice when they might need a question: *are you all right, was that the wrong moment, would you like to stop?* It is not to build a file on them, to catch them out, or to gain an edge in a negotiation they do not know they are in. Keep notes about what you saw and what you guessed, never dossiers on the private lives of named people. If you ever find yourself watching someone in order to use what you see against them, you have left the method of this book behind.

The reading is yours. The person is not.
teach.disconfirm: A good baseline predicts. If, over several meetings, yours keeps failing to predict how someone behaves when nothing in particular is happening, discard it and start again.
teach.pullQuote: The reading is yours. The person is not.

poseGallery.doCaption: A change from his usual, logged as a question.
poseGallery.dontCaption: His usual way of standing, read as a message about you.
poseGallery.annotation: Same crossed arms, two situations. The loose fold is his baseline; the grip and the lifted shoulders are the departure, and even that is only a question.

poseGallery.doCaption: Watching side-on and now and then, the way you watch weather.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Watching hard enough to be noticed, and so measuring your own effect.
poseGallery.annotation: A baseline comes from someone who does not feel watched. If your attention changes their behaviour, the reading is about you.

poseGallery.doCaption: Minute twenty: the same man, settled into his range.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Minute two, read as nervousness about you.
poseGallery.annotation: The first minutes measure the newness of the room. Wait for the settle before you draw the line you will measure from.

poseGallery.doCaption: His neutral: weight on the left leg, hip high, right knee soft.
poseGallery.dontCaption: A textbook neutral laid over everyone.
poseGallery.annotation: There is no universal resting posture. The reference line belongs to the person, not to a figure in a book.

poseGallery.doCaption: Compared with how he looks while listening at ease.
poseGallery.dontCaption: A downward glance mid-answer, read as hiding something.
poseGallery.annotation: Many people look away to think; Glenberg's experiments found that averting the gaze helps people remember. Learn where this person's eyes go when they think before reading anything into it.

poseGallery.doCaption: Checking your own shoulders and breath before reading anyone.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Arriving braced, and finding threat in every face.
poseGallery.annotation: Your own state is the lens. Read your body first, and the room comes into focus.

caseStudy:
Daniel, twenty-nine, has been with Anna for two years when he finally meets her father. Robert is sixty-three, a retired surveyor, and he spends most of the first hour of dinner with his arms folded across his chest, answering Daniel's questions in a sentence or less. Daniel drives home certain that he has been judged and found wanting. For the next month he is stiff and over-polite whenever Anna mentions her father, and when they meet again he talks too much, defending himself against an accusation nobody made.

Anna's brother, Tom, was at the same dinner and saw something else. He has watched his father at a hundred family meals. Robert folds his arms at every table he has ever sat at, and says it is because his back aches if he doesn't. He answers everyone briefly, his own children included. What Tom noticed was different. When Daniel asked about the farm where Robert grew up, his arms came down, he leaned forward and he talked for ten minutes. Then, when Anna mentioned that she and Daniel were thinking of moving abroad for Daniel's work, Robert's hand went to the back of his neck, he stopped eating, and he said nothing for long enough that Anna changed the subject.

Tom did not conclude that his father disliked the move, or Daniel. He noted a change, its timing and how long it lasted, and a week later, walking the dog with Robert, he asked how he felt about Anna possibly moving. Robert was quiet for a while. Then he said he had been dreading it since Anna's mother died, because Anna was the one who rang every Sunday.

Tom told Daniel. On the next visit Daniel did not try to win Robert over. He asked about the farm again, and before they left he mentioned that Anna had already said she would keep the Sunday calls. Robert's arms stayed folded the whole evening. At the door he shook Daniel's hand for a long time.
observe: In a café or on a train, choose one adult who has been settled in their seat for at least ten minutes and who will not notice you. For five minutes, without recording or photographing them, count only how often they touch their face and how often they shift position, and stop at once if they look your way.

On your next video call with someone you know well, write two lines about how they sit and speak in the first two minutes, and two more lines twenty minutes in. Compare the notes afterwards and mark what changed as the call settled.

Pick a long-form interview online in which the guest appears for at least an hour. Watch the first five minutes and a stretch around the forty-minute mark, and write down three things the guest does more in one stretch than in the other.

Before a meeting or a family meal this week, take sixty seconds to note your own baseline: where your shoulders sit, how your breath feels, and what you want to be true about the people you are about to see.

drills.name: The Five-Minute Range
steps: Sit somewhere public where people stay put: a café, a library, a waiting room.
Choose one person who has been settled for at least ten minutes and is absorbed in something. Never photograph or follow anyone; if they notice you, choose someone else or stop.
For five minutes keep a tally of three behaviours only: face touches, posture shifts, and glances away from what they are doing.
Turn each tally into a rate per minute and write a one-line description of their resting range.
Watch for two more minutes and note whether anything falls outside the range you wrote. Most of the time nothing will, and that is the lesson.
variations: Harder: follow two people at neighbouring tables and write a range for each. Note how differently two settled adults can behave.
Lighter: if five minutes feels long, do two minutes on three different days with the same kind of setting, and compare the rates.
Return to the same café at the same hour next week, choose someone similar, and see whether the rates you recorded hold or were peculiar to one person.

drills.name: Two Rooms, One Person
steps: Find two clips of the same public figure in different settings, such as a relaxed talk-show appearance and a formal press conference.
Watch three minutes of each with the sound off.
List what their hands, posture and head do in each setting.
Mark which differences are explained by the setting itself: a lectern, a sofa, a microphone, a hostile room.
Write one sentence on what a reader would get wrong if he used the talk-show baseline to judge the press conference.
variations: Harder: choose a figure whose two settings differ only a little, such as a prepared speech and the questions after it.
With a partner: each watch alone, write your lists, then compare what you each attributed to the setting and what to the person.
Do it for someone you know personally, using two family videos from different occasions, and notice how much of what you think of as their manner belongs to the place.

drills.name: The Settle Curve
steps: Choose a recorded conversation in which you can see one person from the very start: a podcast video, a panel, an interview.
Watch the first eight minutes with a timer running.
Note the minute at which the person first sits back, exhales, or lets their hands come to rest in a habitual place.
Describe their behaviour before and after that moment in two sentences.
Repeat with a second person and see whether they settle sooner or later.
variations: Live version: at your next meeting, note the minute at which you yourself settle, and what changed in your body when you did.
Harder: compare a guest who is clearly comfortable with the host with one who is meeting them for the first time.
Watch the host as well as the guest. Hosts often settle almost at once, because the room is theirs, and the gap between the two curves is worth seeing.

drills.name: Your Own Resting Line
steps: Prop your phone up and record yourself, seated, reading something dull for ten minutes. The recording is for you alone; delete it afterwards if you like.
Play it back at double speed with the sound off.
Count your face touches, posture shifts and leg movements, and turn them into rates.
Write down one habit you did not know you had.
Note how an observer who did not know you might misread that habit.
variations: Second setting: record yourself on a video call as well, and compare your resting rates there with your rates while reading.
Ask someone you trust to name one habit of yours they would call part of your normal, and check it against the recording.
Repeat the recording on a day when you are tired or anxious, and compare the two sets of rates. The difference is your own early-warning sign.

drills.name: Prediction Before Contact
steps: Before you next see someone you meet every week, write three predictions about their resting behaviour: how they will sit, what their hands will do, how fast they will talk.
Put the predictions somewhere you will not reread until afterwards.
During the meeting do not hunt for confirmation; simply be with them.
Afterwards, mark each prediction as a hit, a miss or unclear.
Revise your written baseline for that person in light of the misses.
variations: Add the voice: predict how fast they will talk, how often they will laugh and how long they will pause before answering.
Harder: make predictions about someone you know only slightly, and notice how many more misses you score.
Keep the predictions for a month, across four meetings, and see whether your hit rate rises as your written baseline improves.

quiz.q: A colleague you have never met keeps his arms folded throughout your first meeting. What does the folding tell you on its own?
options: That he is defensive about the topic, or about meeting you
That he disagrees with you but has decided not to say so
Very little, until you know whether he folds his arms at rest
That he feels cold, and that you should adjust the room to suit him
quiz.explain: Folding is one of the most misread postures because it appears in so many resting baselines. Without knowing how he sits when nothing is at stake, you cannot tell a habit from a reaction. A cold room is a fair alternative hypothesis, but it is still a hypothesis, not something the folding tells you.

quiz.q: Why does Aldert Vrij criticise baselining someone during small talk and then comparing them during difficult questions?
options: Small talk produces too little behaviour to measure reliably, so any baseline taken from it is mostly noise
People lie during small talk as well, so the baseline already contains the very behaviour you are trying to detect
Baselines can only be taken reliably from video, because live observers miss most of what happens in real time
The two conversations differ in stakes and difficulty, so behaviour would change even in an honest person
quiz.explain: The comparison mixes up the thing you care about with everything else that changes between the two conversations. Hard questions are harder, more closely watched and more emotional for anyone. A useful baseline is taken under conditions as close as possible to the moment you want to interpret.

quiz.q: At lunch, a usually animated friend tells a story about his weekend with his hands moving freely. When someone asks whether he has heard back about the promotion, his hands drop into his lap and stay there for the next few minutes while he answers briefly. What is the most defensible note to make?
options: He didn't get the promotion and is hiding it, so you should change the subject to spare him
He is angry with the person who asked, and the stillness is his way of controlling it
His gestures stopped right after the promotion question and stayed down; worth a gentle private question later
Nothing, because hands resting in the lap is a normal posture and carries no meaning at all
quiz.explain: This note records change, timing and duration without claiming to know the cause. The last option ignores that the stillness departs from his own animated baseline, which is exactly what makes it informative. The first two leap to a meaning the body cannot supply.

quiz.q: In an observational study of medical students during lectures, roughly how often did people touch their own faces?
options: About 23 times an hour
About twice an hour
About once every ten minutes
Almost never, unless anxious
quiz.explain: Kwok and colleagues counted an average of 23 face touches per hour among attentive students. The figure sets the background rate: one face touch, or several, means nothing on its own. What can mean something is a change in rate for a particular person, tied to a particular moment.

quiz.q: Research on thin slices shows that observers can predict some outcomes from a few seconds of silent video. What follows for reading a stranger you have just met?
options: That first impressions are reliable enough that you can usually trust your first read
That impressions agree across observers, not that one quick read of someone's feelings is right
That you should only try to read people in the first thirty seconds of meeting them
That thin slices only work when the sound is on and the observer can hear the voice
quiz.explain: The studies by Ambady and Rosenthal concern broad, stable impressions such as warmth, pooled across several observers. They do not show that one observer can read one person's passing state at a glance. The first minutes of an encounter are also when behaviour is least like a person's baseline.

quiz.q: You arrive at a performance review exhausted after a sleepless night with a sick child. Your manager seems curt, and you sense disapproval in every pause. What should you do first?
options: Address the disapproval directly, so that it does not hang over the whole review
Recognise that your own state is colouring what you see, and hold the reading loosely
Match her curtness, so that she can see you are not intimidated by her manner
Assume she has bad news for you, and prepare your arguments before she says it
quiz.explain: Fatigue and anxiety tilt readings toward threat, an effect Joseph Forgas studied as affect infusion. Your own baseline is off, so your reading of hers is unreliable. That does not mean ignoring what you notice; it means treating it as a guess until you can compare it with how she usually is in reviews.

quiz.q: You have worked beside a colleague for a year. Over the last month he has started arriving late, eating lunch alone and keeping his door shut. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is clearly unhappy in his job, so the kind thing is to raise it with his line manager at once
A sustained change from a long baseline earns a gentle, private question, not a conclusion
Nothing can be read from behaviour, so the best course is to ignore the change entirely
He is probably hiding something, so it is wise to keep an eye on him for a few weeks
quiz.explain: A long, well-sampled baseline is exactly what makes a sustained change worth noticing. It still tells you only that something has changed, not what, so the right response is an open question in private.

quiz.q: Why does this chapter advise discounting the first minutes of an encounter when you take someone's baseline?
options: Because people deliberately perform for strangers early on and relax only once they forget
Because the first minutes are when people are most honest, before they think to hide anything
Because a new room and a new person unsettle almost everyone, so you would be measuring novelty
Because research shows that baselines can only be taken reliably after at least an hour together
quiz.explain: Almost everyone is less settled at the start of an encounter than later. A baseline taken in those minutes measures the room and the novelty, and the later settling can then be misread as the person warming to you.

quiz.q: Which of these is a baseline written the way this chapter recommends?
options: He is a nervous, fidgety type who never seems to relax in meetings with senior people
He seemed defensive and closed off in the first few minutes, though he got better later
He is a confident man whose body language shows that he is comfortable with any authority
Seated at his desk, he touches his face about twice a minute and rests his chin on his hand
quiz.explain: A baseline describes the body, in a named setting, as a range or rate. Labels such as nervous, defensive or confident are interpretations, and they smuggle the conclusion into the very thing you will later compare against.

quiz.q: You meet your partner's oldest friend for the first time at a loud birthday party. He is brief with you and keeps glancing at the door. What is the most defensible reading?
options: He dislikes you, since a man who glances at the door wants the conversation to end
You have no baseline for him, so note it, hold it loosely and judge him on later meetings
He is nervous about meeting you, which shows that he cares about your partner's opinion
He is hiding something about your partner, since glancing away is a classic sign of guilt
quiz.explain: You have one sample, in a noisy setting, taken in the first minutes of meeting. Any reading of him as a person would be built on a template, so the honest course is to hold it loosely and let later meetings show you his range.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific person you see at least once a week: a colleague, a parent, a flatmate. Write their baseline as precisely as you can: how they sit or stand, what their hands do, how fast they talk, where their eyes go when they think. Then describe one specific occasion when you misread them because you compared them with how you expected a person to behave rather than with how they usually are. What did you conclude, what was actually going on, and how did you find out?
reflection.guidance: Write the baseline in plain physical language, as if for someone who has never met this person: *sits sideways with one foot on the rung of the chair*, not *relaxed*. For the misreading, name the moment, what you saw, and the conclusion you drew before you knew better. Most people find the second part uncomfortable, which is a sign it is worth doing. If no misreading comes to mind, choose the person you are surest you understand and ask what you would see if they were struggling. Given how they usually are, would you notice?

failureMode: The most common misuse of this chapter is to learn the word baseline and skip the work. A reader watches someone for two minutes, decides that is their normal, and from then on treats every difference as a signal. He has replaced one template with another, smaller one, built from a sample too short to mean anything and usually taken in the very minutes when the other person was least settled. The result is worse than having no baseline, because it feels like method. The second failure is subtler: treating a departure as an answer. A change from baseline tells you that something registered. It does not tell you what, and the likeliest explanations are often mundane: a sore back, a full bladder, a memory, a draught. If you catch yourself thinking *he departed from baseline, so he is upset about this*, stop at the comma. A departure earns a question, never a conclusion.

moreCases.title: The quiet new starter
moreCases.scene:
Priya joins a design team of eight on a Monday. In her first three team meetings she sits at the end of the table, keeps her
  laptop half closed, speaks once or twice, and answers questions in a sentence. Her manager, Gareth, has run the team for six years. He
  is used to new hires who arrive keen, talk too much in the first fortnight, and then settle down. By the second Friday he has decided
  that Priya is either unhappy or not very interested, and he mentions to his own manager that the hire may have been a mistake.

  Mark, who sits next to Priya, sees the same meetings and something else. In their one-to-one conversations at the coffee machine she
  talks quickly and laughs easily. In the meetings, she writes constantly. On Thursday, when the team discussed a client's complaint, she
  stopped writing, looked up, and asked the only question in the room that the client had actually raised. Mark also notices that the
  two other people on the team who came from agencies behaved much the same way in their first weeks, because in their old jobs junior
  staff did not speak in front of clients. Both of them are now among the most talkative people on the team. Mark mentions none of this,
  because nobody asks him, and because he assumes Gareth has seen what he has.
moreCases.misread: Gareth compared Priya with a template built from his own past hires, and read the difference as a message about her commitment. He also took his sample in the first ten days, when almost everyone is least settled, and in a single setting. Nothing in her behaviour had departed from anything, because he had never seen her baseline. And the costs of his reading were real: a word to his own manager that could have followed Priya through her probation, built on nothing but how she sat in three meetings.
moreCases.betterRead: Mark had two settings to compare and noticed that the difference between them was the room, not the person. He saw a change within the meetings that mattered: the moment she stopped writing and asked the question. A careful observer would note Priya's meeting range, wait a month before trusting it, and, if worried, simply ask her how she was finding the team. Gareth did ask, in the end. She said she was enjoying it and was used to keeping quiet until she knew how a team worked.

moreCases.title: The father who stopped whistling
moreCases.scene:
Joe, thirty-four, visits his father most Sundays. For as long as he can remember, his dad has whistled while he works in the
  garage, talked to the radio during the football results, and come in from the car the moment it is parked. Over two months Joe notices
  that the whistling has stopped. His father now sits in the parked car for several minutes before coming inside, and he has started
  leaving the radio off.

  None of these would mean anything in a stranger. Plenty of men sit in their cars, and plenty never whistle. Joe's sister, who visits
  less often, thinks their father seems fine: he is polite, he asks after the children, he makes the tea. Joe is inclined to agree with
  her, and to put the change down to age. His father is sixty-eight. Men slow down. And raising it feels absurd: what would he say, that
  his dad has stopped whistling? He imagines the look he would get. For three more Sundays he says nothing, and drives home each time with
  a vague unease he cannot quite name. On the fourth Sunday his father forgets that the grandchildren are coming, which he has never done
  before, and spends most of the afternoon in the garden on his own.
moreCases.misread: The misreading here is not an over-reading but an under-reading. Having no template to compare with, Joe's sister saw an ordinary older man behaving normally. Joe had a long baseline and was tempted to explain away the departure from it, because noticing it meant having an awkward conversation. This is the quieter failure of reading, and probably the commoner one between men who love each other: seeing the change clearly, and talking yourself out of it, because the question feels too big for the evidence.
moreCases.betterRead: A long baseline is the most valuable thing in this chapter, and the change Joe saw is exactly what it is for: three behaviours, each part of his father's range for decades, all gone at once, and staying gone. The chapter's rule still applies. A departure earns a question, not a conclusion. Joe chose a moment in the garage, side by side, and said that he had noticed his dad was not whistling any more. After a pause his father told him that the business he had helped a friend start was failing and that he had lent money he could not afford to lose. The baseline did not tell Joe what was wrong. It told him when to ask.

moreCases.title: Training and matches
moreCases.scene:
Dev coaches a Sunday-league football team. One of his centre backs, Callum, is the hardest worker in training: first to every loose
  ball, loud, constantly organising the players around him. In matches he is quieter for the first twenty minutes, hangs a few yards
  deeper, and rarely shouts. After a heavy defeat, two of the senior players tell Dev that Callum does not seem up for games and should
  be dropped.

  Dev has seen the pattern for two seasons. He goes back over the match footage he films on his phone and counts. In every game, Callum's
  first twenty minutes look the same, and in every game, his touches, tackles and shouting rise sharply after that, often peaking in the
  last quarter of an hour, when others are tiring. In the defeat, he played exactly as he always does. The difference in that match was
  that the team conceded twice in the first fifteen minutes. Dev also remembers that Callum works nights on a Saturday, arrives at the
  ground with barely enough time to change, and says he needs a few minutes of the game to wake up. None of this is visible from the
  touchline. All of it is part of the man's baseline on a match day.
moreCases.misread: The senior players used Callum's training baseline to judge his match behaviour. Training and matches are different settings, with different stakes and different rhythms, and he has a baseline for each. They also read a single game's result back into his body: because the team lost early, his usual slow start looked like a lack of commitment. And they reasoned from the outcome back to the body, which is the most tempting error in sport: when things go badly, every ordinary habit starts to look like the cause.
moreCases.betterRead: Dev kept the two baselines separate and checked the match one against footage rather than memory. He found that Callum's slow start was part of his normal range in games, and that nothing in the defeat departed from it. A coach who knows that can plan for it, perhaps by pairing Callum with a vocal partner in the opening minutes, instead of dropping a player for being exactly who he always is. He also told the two senior players what he had found, and showed them the counts, which did more to settle the dressing room than any speech about commitment.

moreCases.title: The interviewer who had not slept
moreCases.scene:
Helen interviews five candidates on a Thursday after a night spent mostly awake with a sick toddler. She notices that she is short-
  tempered on the drive in, but thinks no more of it. The first two candidates seem guarded to her: one folds his arms, the other keeps
  his answers brief. The third, who laughs a lot and leans forward, seems warm and open, and she rates him highest. By the afternoon she
  has had coffee and lunch, and the last two candidates both seem perfectly pleasant.

  Her colleague Sam sat in on all five interviews and scored them against the agreed questions. His scores put the first candidate
  joint top and the third in the middle. When they compare notes, Helen cannot point to anything in the first candidate's answers that
  was weak. She remembers his folded arms and his flat tone, and that is all. She had written "cold" in the margin of her sheet beside his
  name, and "guarded?" beside the second candidate's, and nothing at all beside the content of either man's answers. When she tries to say why she liked the third candidate, she
  describes his energy, his laugh and the way he leaned in. Sam points out that two of the third candidate's answers to the technical
  questions were wrong.
moreCases.misread: Helen read the candidates without first reading herself. Tired and on edge, she saw the morning candidates through her own mood, and the one whose manner most soothed her, not the one who answered best, rose to the top. She also had no baseline for any of them: the folded arms and the brief answers were compared with an imagined ideal candidate, not with the man himself.
moreCases.betterRead: The chapter's last two teaching points apply directly. Your own state is the first baseline to take, and a morning after a sleepless night is a reason to lean harder on structure: score against the agreed criteria before forming an overall impression, and treat strong likes and dislikes as data about yourself. Helen and Sam agreed to re-interview the first candidate on a Monday. He folded his arms again, answered as briefly, and was offered the job. Helen now checks her own state before an interview day, and when it is poor she says so to her co-interviewer and asks him to watch her scoring as well as the candidates.

workedReading.title: A friend at the pub
workedReading.scene: Sam and Rich have met for a drink on the first Friday of the month for nine years. Tonight the pub is a new one, chosen because their usual place has closed for refurbishment. Rich arrives ten minutes late, which he never is, orders a soft drink rather than his usual pint, and spends the first half hour talking about work in a flat voice, glancing at his phone face down on the table. When Sam mentions that his own son has just started secondary school, Rich goes quiet, rubs the back of his neck and changes the subject to football. Later, while Sam is at the bar, he sees Rich turn the phone over, read something, and put it face down again without replying. By ten o'clock Rich says he ought to get back, which in nine years he has never said before half past eleven.

steps.label: Check yourself
steps.text: Before reading Rich, Sam notices his own state. He has had a good week and is in the mood for a long, loud evening. That matters: a man who wants a lively night will see a quiet friend as a problem to be fixed. Sam also notices that he is slightly irritated by the late arrival, which will make him more likely to read the rest of the evening as a slight. Naming both does not remove them, but it lets him discount his first impressions a little, the way a navigator corrects for a compass he knows is off.

steps.label: Recall the range
steps.text: Sam knows Rich's baseline well, across years and settings. Rich is usually punctual, drinks one or two pints, talks a lot about work and complains about it cheerfully, checks his phone rarely when out, and asks about Sam's family. He goes quiet when he is tired, and he rubs his neck when his back is playing up after five-a-side. That last habit is part of his range, not outside it. What Sam does not have is a baseline for Rich in this particular pub, or for Rich on a night after a hard week at home, because he has never needed one. He knows the man well; he knows the setting not at all.

steps.label: Describe the change
steps.text: In plain terms: he arrived late, chose a soft drink, spoke more flatly than usual about work, kept his phone on the table and glanced at it often, and went quiet with his hand on his neck when Sam mentioned his son's new school. The timing of that last change is the sharpest data point of the evening: it followed a specific topic within a second or two. The other changes were there from the moment he arrived, which suggests they belong to his evening rather than to anything Sam said. Separating the two kinds of change is half the work.

steps.label: Weigh the context
steps.text: Several things are different tonight that have nothing to do with Rich's inner life. It is a new pub, which unsettles almost everyone for a while. He may be driving, which would explain the soft drink. He may be expecting a call, which would explain the phone. Each departure has a dull rival explanation, and Sam should hold those first. The reaction to the school topic has fewer obvious rivals. Even so, a neck rub on its own would be nothing, given Rich's back; it is the silence and the change of subject that come with it, at that moment, that make it worth holding onto.

steps.label: Generate hypotheses
steps.text: Sam writes nothing down, but he holds several possibilities at once rather than one. Rich is tired and driving. Rich is waiting for news, perhaps medical, perhaps about work. Something about children or schools is painful at the moment: Rich and his partner have spoken before about wanting a child. Or he is simply having a flat week. No single sign points to one of these; the cluster, and especially the timing, makes the third worth keeping in mind.

steps.label: Test gently
steps.text: The test is not a probing question about children. It is an open door: later, walking to the station side by side, Sam says that Rich seemed a bit far away tonight and asks whether everything is all right. If Rich says he is fine and talks about the match, Sam lets it go and notes that the evening was one off night. If he says more, Sam listens. Either answer is evidence, and Sam resolves in advance to accept the first one if that is the one he gets, rather than pressing until he hears what he expected. What Sam must not do is announce a conclusion, such as telling Rich he seems upset about kids, which would put Rich in the position of confirming or denying something Sam has guessed from his body.

steps.label: Update the baseline
steps.text: Rich said that they had had a second miscarriage the month before, that he was driving because his partner was not up to coming out, and that he was waiting for her to text. Sam did not need to read any of that from Rich's body, and could not have. What the reading did was tell him when to open the door, and how gently. He also learned something lasting about his friend: that in a hard month Rich keeps coming out, keeps talking about work, and goes quiet only at the edge of the thing that hurts.

moreFailures.title: Taking the baseline on a bad day
moreFailures.body: A baseline sampled during an unusual stretch of someone's life becomes the yardstick against which their ordinary life looks strange. A manager who first meets a new report during the week of a house move, a man who first spends time with his partner's family over a tense Christmas, a coach who first sees a player while he is carrying an injury: each learns a version of the person that is itself a departure. Then, when the person recovers, their normal behaviour looks like a change. The defence is to treat any baseline as provisional until you have seen it hold across several occasions and at least two settings, and to ask, early on, whether this is a typical week for them.

moreFailures.title: Pretending to baseline strangers
moreFailures.body: Some readers, having learned this chapter, try to apply it to everyone they meet for five minutes: the barista, the man across the train carriage, the salesperson. They glance, form an impression of the person's normal, and then read every small movement against it. This is the old template in disguise. With strangers you rarely have a baseline at all, and the honest move is to admit it: lean on context, hold your readings loosely, and, where something matters, ask. Precision you have not earned is worse than none, because it feels like knowledge. A barista who seems curt with you may be forty orders into a rush, nursing a headache, or simply someone who is brief with everyone; you have no way of telling which, and no need to. The discipline of this chapter is as much about knowing when you do not have a baseline as about building one when you can.

moreFailures.title: Turning attention into surveillance
moreFailures.body: Knowing someone's baseline well gives you a kind of power over them, and it can curdle. A partner who starts logging when the other checks their phone, how long they spend in the shower, and which messages make them smile is not reading carefully; he is building a case. The same habits that make you a good friend, noticing change and asking about it, become controlling when they are used to monitor, to catch out or to confirm a suspicion. The test is simple. Would the other person be comfortable knowing exactly what you track and why? If not, stop. Attention is not permission. Where you have a genuine worry about someone close to you, the remedy is the same as everywhere else in this book: say what you have noticed, plainly and kindly, and ask. A question respects the other person as the authority on their own life. A dossier does not.

moreFailures.title: Mistaking your baseline of a person for the person
moreFailures.body: After years together it is easy to believe you know exactly how someone is, and to stop looking. The danger is that you go on reading the person you knew rather than the person in front of you. A wife who has always been quiet at parties and is now quieter still, a friend who used to be the loudest in the group and has gradually become the most thoughtful, a father who has grown gentler with age: each may be read against a picture that is years out of date. The changes may be good ones. They may be signs of strain. You will not know which unless you keep noticing, and you will not notice if you think you already know. Revisit your baselines of the people closest to you at least once a year, as deliberately as you would revisit an old map before a journey.

questions.q: How long does it take to establish someone's baseline?
questions.a: Longer than most people think, and less long than it sounds. For a person who is settled in one setting, such as a colleague at their desk, twenty or thirty minutes of side-on attention will give you a rough range for things like posture, face-touching and how often they look away. For a person you want to read across settings, you need to see them in several, on several days. A useful rule of thumb is three occasions and two settings before you trust the range, and to discard the first ten minutes of any encounter. Long familiarity helps, but only if you keep updating, because people change. It also helps to write a baseline down, even in a line or two, because memory quietly edits itself to fit whatever you now believe about someone. A note made in March is a far better witness in June than your recollection of March.

questions.q: What if I only meet someone once, for an interview or a negotiation?
questions.a: Then you have a baseline for the encounter, not for the person, and you should treat it that way. Let the first minutes pass before you start comparing, use the calmer middle of the conversation as your reference, and compare like with like: answers to similar questions, rather than small talk with hard questions. Hold every reading more loosely than you would with someone you know. Most importantly, remember that the person is also baselining you, and also getting it wrong. Structure, clear questions and a willingness to ask what someone meant will serve you better than any reading of their body. If a single meeting really matters, such as a negotiation that will run over several sessions, treat the first as the baseline and save your firmer readings for the second and third, when you have something to compare against.

questions.q: Isn't watching people this closely a bit creepy?
questions.a: It can be, which is why the chapter insists on side-on attention, the way you notice weather, rather than staring. You are already watching people; everyone is, all the time, and mostly badly. Learning to do it well is mostly about doing less of it at any one moment and more of it over time. The difference between attention and surveillance lies in purpose and proportion. Attention is in the service of understanding and responding to someone. Surveillance is in the service of catching them out. Never record people without consent, never follow anyone, and never use what you notice to manipulate.

questions.q: Do people have baselines for voice and speech, as well as for the body?
questions.a: Yes, and they are often more useful. Speaking rate, pitch, loudness, how long someone pauses before answering, how often they laugh, and even their typical sentence length all have ranges that are stable for the person and vary widely between people. A man who normally answers in a sentence is not being curt when he does so with you. The chapter on the voice later in this part takes this further. The same rules apply: discount the first minutes, compare like with like, and note change, timing and duration before you interpret.

questions.q: What if someone's baseline includes a lot of movement, like constant fidgeting?
questions.a: Then movement is their normal, and stillness may be the departure worth noticing. Many people, including many autistic people and people with ADHD, move a great deal as part of how they concentrate or regulate themselves. Reading that movement against a still template produces a steady stream of false alarms: nervousness, boredom, dishonesty. Learn their range like anyone else's. Part V's chapters on neurodivergence and masking explain why this matters so much, and why asking someone to sit still can cost them more than it seems.

questions.q: Can I use this on myself, to notice when I am not doing well?
questions.a: That is one of its best uses, and Part II of this book builds a whole early-warning system around it. Your own baseline is the one you can sample most often and in the most settings. Notice how you sleep, how much you eat, how often you see friends, how your shoulders sit at the end of a working day, how quickly you snap. When several of these drift together, and stay drifted for a couple of weeks, take it as seriously as you would a change in a friend. The people closest to you often see your departures before you do, so it is worth asking one of them, in a good week, what they would notice first if you were struggling.

watch.title: Former FBI Agent Explains How to Read Body Language
watch.notice: Joe Navarro walks through the behaviours he looks for. Notice how often he compares a person with their own normal behaviour, and where a single cue is being asked to carry more weight than this chapter would allow.

watch.title: Sherlock and John's First Meeting
watch.notice: Sherlock reads a stranger in seconds. Enjoy it, and notice what he never has: a baseline. A real reader would need to see how John behaves on an ordinary day before trusting any of it.

reviewPrompt: Choose one person you will see in the next two days and, before you meet, write three predictions about their resting behaviour. Afterwards, score each as a hit or a miss and rewrite each miss as a better description.
